articles.title: Are you being exploited by AI-powered surveillance pricing?
articles.summary: The FTC ordered Mastercard, Chase, and other companies to turn over information on their dynamic pricing products.
articles.body: Nearly a decade ago, Uber revealed that customers are more willing to pay surge prices when their phones are about to die. That data point sparked a pervasive belief that Uber and other ridehailing apps use algorithms to tailor each passenger’s price to their behavior and willingness to pay — a practice known as “surveillance pricing.” A related myth — that airlines use your search history to jack up prices for flights you’re interested in — is similarly ubiquitous even though it’s not true. Surveillance pricing may not be widespread yet, but experts say it’s on the horizon, and consultants are starting to offer surveillance pricing models to businesses across various industries. The Federal Trade Commission announced today that it’s ordering eight companies that offer AI surveillance pricing products and services to turn over information about the impact these pricing schemes have on privacy, competition, and consumer protection, the FTC announced today. Surveillance pricing — often called “dynamic pricing,” “personalized pricing,” or “price optimization” — involves offering individual consumers different prices for the same products based on a combination of factors, including the device they’re shopping on, their location, demographic information, credit history, and browsing and shopping history. “Firms that harvest Americans’ personal data can put people’s privacy at risk. Now firms could be exploiting this vast trove of personal information to charge people higher prices,” FTC Chair Lina Khan said in a statement. “Americans deserve to know whether businesses are using detailed consumer data to deploy surveillance pricing, and the FTC’s inquiry will shed light on this shadowy ecosystem of pricing middlemen.” Companies have already experimented with implementing Uber-style surge pricing. JetBlue quietly implemented “peak” and “off-peak” pricing to its checked bag fees in March. Walmart plans on bringing digital price tags to 2,300 stores over the next several years that will let it change products’ prices depending on a number of factors, including the weather, whether items are closer to their expiration date, and more. Wendy’s said it would roll out “dynamic pricing” in 2025. Amazon had a secret algorithm called Project Nessie that let it gauge how much it could raise its prices before its competitors took notice and changed theirs, too. [Media: These pricing models, while variable, are a bit different from surveillance pricing, which relies on using an individual consumer’s information to determine how much they’re willing to pay for a specific product. The FTC orders were sent to Mastercard, Revionics, Bloomreach, Chase, Task, Pros, Accenture, and McKinsey & Co., the FTC announced in a press release. They were issued under the FTC’s 6(b) authority, which lets it conduct studies without any specific law enforcement purpose. “These eight firms advertise their use of AI and machine learning as part of the services they offer, often claiming they can use historical and real-time customer information to drive unique purchasing experiences,” an FTC official said on a call with reporters ahead of the announcement, adding that none of the firms issued orders have been accused of any wrongdoing. “What we’re trying to do is lift the hood on opaque practices that have the potential to profoundly reshape how consumers purchase goods and services. We want to make sure that surveillance pricing isn’t resulting in harm to certain communities, like women and rural consumers.” The companies are being asked to turn over information on: * Types of surveillance pricing products and services they’ve produced, developed, or licensed to a third party * Data sources used for each product or service * Who they’re offering surveillance pricing products and services to * How this impacts surveilled consumers and pricing On a call with reporters, an FTC official said a study is necessary because the extent to which businesses use surveillance pricing is currently unknown. Media reports suggest that companies across a wide variety of sectors — including grocery stores, restaurant chains, travel, and hospitality — are considering implementing surveillance pricing or have already done so. “The technology is there, the incentives are there, the data certainly is there to do this targeting,” the FTC official told reporters. “And now we actually see this industry of consultancies potentially offer to help companies personalize pricing, which gives us a strong reason to believe that this practice is likely to grow.”

articles.title: The Nvidia AI antitrust investigation is ‘escalating,’ reports Bloomberg
articles.summary: Nvidia and other companies have received subpoenas indicating a Department of Justice antitrust investigation into its AI chip business is moving forward.
articles.body: An antitrust investigation by the Department of Justice focusing on Nvidia’s AI dominance as the hardware company of choice is escalating, reports Bloomberg. The outlet reports that Nvidia and other companies have received legally binding requests for information as its sources say regulators are investigating whether Nvidia is “making it harder to switch to other suppliers and penalizes buyers that don’t exclusively use its artificial intelligence chips.” “Nvidia wins on merit, as reflected in our benchmark results and value to customers, and customers can choose whatever solution is best for them. We have inquired with the U.S. Department of Justice and have not been subpoenaed. Nonetheless, we are happy to answer any questions regulators may have about our business,” said Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo, as reported previously by CNBC. Earlier this summer, Nvidia had overtaken Microsoft as the world’s most valuable company, but now it trails both Microsoft and Apple. Before the subpoenas were reported on Tuesday afternoon, its share price dropped more than 9 percent, wiping out about $279 billion in market value in one day. But as Bloomberg notes, Nvidia’s stock is still up more than double this year as the AI boom has fueled sales of the company’s pricey chips, even after a report by The Information a few weeks ago saying that its upcoming Blackwell series of AI chips may be delayed “by three months or more due to design flaws.” Update, September 4th: Added Nvidia statement previously reported by CNBC.

articles.title: BH terá multa de até R$ 1 mil para motos com barulho acima do permitido; veja quando regra entra em vigor | G1
articles.standfirst: Lei sancionada pelo prefeito Álvaro Damião prevê multa de R$ 500, que pode dobrar em caso de reincidência. Nova regra começa a valer em 90 dias.
articles.summary: Lei sancionada pelo prefeito Álvaro Damião prevê multa de R$ 500, que pode dobrar em caso de reincidência. Nova regra começa a valer em 90 dias.
articles.body:
Imagem ilustrativa de motocicletas e carros — Foto: Globo/ Reprodução

Motociclistas que circularem por Belo Horizonte com veículos que emitam barulho acima dos limites permitidos poderão ser multados em até R$ 1 mil. A medida está prevista em uma lei sancionada pelo prefeito Álvaro Damião (União Brasil) e publicada no Diário Oficial do Município nesta quarta-feira (28).

A nova legislação estabelece multa de R$ 500 para quem descumprir as regras, valor que pode chegar a R$ 1 mil em caso de reincidência no período de 12 meses. A cobrança começa a valer 90 dias após a publicação da lei.

A medida vale para motocicletas, motonetas, ciclomotores e outros veículos motorizados de duas rodas que ultrapassem os limites de ruído estabelecidos pelas normas brasileiras.

A lei também prevê punições para veículos com sistemas de escapamento que estejam em desacordo com as exigências ambientais de controle de ruídos e emissão de poluentes.

A multa será administrativa e poderá ser aplicada independentemente de outras penalidades previstas no Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB).

A legislação teve origem em um projeto apresentado pelo vereador Sargento Jalyson (PL), mas foi sancionada com veto parcial do prefeito Álvaro Damião.

O trecho retirado considerava irregulares escapamentos adulterados, defeituosos, modificados ou com descarga livre.

Na justificativa, o prefeito argumentou que nem toda alteração no escapamento é proibida, já que algumas modificações são autorizadas pela legislação brasileira.

Damião também considerou que a definição dessas irregularidades poderia invadir a competência da União para legislar sobre trânsito.

O veto ainda será analisado por uma comissão especial da Câmara Municipal de Belo Horizonte e, posteriormente, submetido à votação dos vereadores. Para derrubar a decisão do prefeito, serão necessários pelo menos 21 votos contrários ao veto.

A nova lei permite que a Prefeitura de Belo Horizonte estabeleça parcerias com órgãos públicos municipais, estaduais e federais para promover ações de fiscalização e conscientização sobre a poluição sonora.

Segundo o vereador Sargento Jalyson, autor do projeto, a proposta busca reduzir os transtornos causados pelo excesso de barulho de motocicletas e proteger a saúde e a qualidade de vida dos moradores.

Na justificativa apresentada à Câmara, o parlamentar também destacou os impactos ambientais de escapamentos irregulares, que podem aumentar a emissão de gases poluentes.

A legislação não detalha, no texto divulgado pela Câmara, como será feita a medição dos ruídos durante a fiscalização.

articles.title: Alunos de universidade do Paraná denunciam ataques a bolsistas e mensagens de cunho nazista em conversas online após eleições | G1
articles.standfirst: Nas mensagens, estudantes fazem comentários ofensivos contra estudantes que ingressaram na instituição por meio de programas sociais. Ministério Público Federal afirma que analisa denúncia feita por alunos.
articles.summary: Nas mensagens, estudantes fazem comentários ofensivos contra estudantes que ingressaram na instituição por meio de programas sociais.
articles.body:
Mensagens foram enviadas em um aplicativo de mensagens — Foto: Unsplash

Alunos de uma universidade privada de Maringá , no Norte do Paraná, denunciaram ao Ministério Público Federal (MPF) uma série de mensagens com cunho nazista e ataques a bolsistas que circularam em um grupo de conversas de uma turma da instituição.

As mensagens foram enviadas no último domingo (25) por estudantes de medicina, depois que o resultado das eleições presidenciais foi divulgado.

Nelas, alunos fazem comentários ofensivos contra estudantes que ingressaram na universidade por meio de programas sociais, como o Programa Universidade para Todos (ProUni).

Em uma das publicações, um estudante sugere superioridade em relação aos bolsistas ao comparar quem paga a mensalidade com quem conquistou a vaga por seleção acadêmica de programas sociais.

"Quem paga trabalhou e tem 15 mil [reais] por mês para pagar >>>>>>> Quem passou numa provinha", escreveu um outro estudante.

Além disso, imagens e expressões associadas ao nazismo também foram compartilhadas nos grupos.

Outra aluna criticou as ofensas e ressaltou que todos terão a mesma formação, independentemente da forma de ingresso. "Virou bonito ofender quem não tem dinheiro para pagar toda a mensalidade como vocês? Todo mundo aqui vai sair com CRM [registro profissional de medicina]", disse.

O g1 optou por não identificar os alunos por se tratar de um tema sensível, que ainda está sendo investigado pelos órgãos responsáveis, e que pode envolver menores de idade.

O Ministério Público Federal informou que analisa a denúncia enviada pelos alunos.

Ao g1, um estudante informou que tanto os universitários que fizeram as ofensas quanto aqueles que foram alvos das mensagens não estão frequentando a instituição desde a repercussão do caso.

"É um clima hostil na faculdade, um clima hostil nos grupos, que vai muito além de divergências políticas. Parece que o contexto da eleição foi apenas um pretexto para eles extravasarem o ódio às pessoas mais pobres", disse o estudante, que preferiu não ser identificado.

A UniCesumar, instituição em que os alunos estudam, ressaltou que os grupos nos quais circularam as mensagens não são canais oficiais da universidade. Além disso, informou que abriu uma sindicância para apurar o caso e tomar as medidas necessárias. Confira a nota completa abaixo.

O Conselho Regional de Medicina (CRM) disse que adotará providências cabíveis e acompanhará os desdobramentos do caso.

Em nota, a UniCesumar afirmou que repudia qualquer forma de discriminação ou preconceito. Veja na íntegra:

"A UniCesumar reafirma seu compromisso com a ética, com a responsabilidade, e com o respeito à vida e aos valores que orientam a formação de seus estudantes, e repudia veementemente qualquer forma de discriminação ou preconceito.

A universidade esclarece que abriu sindicância para apuração do caso, e adotará todas as providências cabíveis, em conformidade com seus regulamentos internos e princípios éticos.

Cumpre ainda informar que o grupo de WhatsApp, no qual circularam mensagens discriminatórias não tem qualquer vínculo com a Instituição, não se tratando de canal oficial desta.

E, considerando que o acesso ao grupo ocorre mediante o convite dos próprios participantes e, não é restrito à comunidade acadêmica, a universidade consegue identificar apenas os integrantes que fazem parte de seu corpo discente, cujos dados não serão compartilhados por questões legais e éticas relativas à confidencialidade.

A UniCesumar ressalta que o Núcleo de Apoio ao Estudante de Medicina (NAEME) permanece à disposição dos alunos para oferecer acolhimento, orientação e suporte".

O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) informou que as atitudes descritas ferem os princípios do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina. Confira:

"Tais atitudes ferem diretamente os princípios fundamentais do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina, segundo os quais o estudante deve estar a serviço da saúde do ser humano e da coletividade, exercendo suas atividades sem discriminação de qualquer natureza.

A escolha pela Medicina exige compromissos humanísticos e humanitários, pautados pela promoção do bem-estar físico, mental e social dos indivíduos e da coletividade. Atitudes discriminatórias são incompatíveis com esses valores e não devem ser toleradas no ambiente de formação médica.

O CRM-PR adotará todas as providências cabíveis no âmbito de suas atribuições institucionais e acompanhará o desdobramento do caso, contribuindo para que haja uma apuração rigorosa e transparente dos fatos pelas instâncias competentes".

articles.title: Hackers target US campaign finance system days before midterm elections
articles.summary: An FEC email said a ‘bad actor’ tried to breach its systems as the US prepares for its most expensive elections ever.
articles.body:
Hackers have reportedly targeted the US Federal Election Commission’s (FEC) website, disrupting campaign financing disclosures just days before the midterm elections.

An FEC email sent to a campaign compliance firm reportedly read, “We have a bad actor trying to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily suspend our web-facing services,” according to Reuters news agency.

The outage prevents organisations from filing the FEC’s 24 and 48-hour spending reports, which track how political groups and candidates are spending on specific races.

A status message on the FEC website showed the system was down after 10.15pm EST on Monday (2.15am GMT on Tuesday).

An update was posted on Tuesday at 8.17pm EST, reading, “The issue has been identified and a fix is being implemented.”

The FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency both referred questions to the FEC.

The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections, but the reported hack comes as so-called Super PACs and dark money groups are spending record sums in the final days before the midterm elections on November 3.

Democratic FEC Commissioner Dara Lindenbaum wrote on X, “This has NOTHING to do with voter files or voter registration. Those are maintained by the states. The FEC only handles federal campaign finance findings.

“We are working hard to restore the systems as soon as possible.”

The midterms are now the most expensive US elections in history, with roughly $11.21bn spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political advertising tracker AdImpact.

That surpasses the previous record of $11.2bn spent in the 2024 elections – including $3.2bn in the presidential race between President Donald Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to AdImpact figures.

Much of the spending is being done by super PACs – independent political committees which can accept unlimited amounts of money from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend it on campaigns, with few restrictions.

Super PACs and dark money groups have spent an average of $50m per day over the past week, according to Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog group OpenSecrets.

“It’s a big deal,” Glavin said. “In the last days of the election, this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money is being spent.”

articles.title: How a grocery merger could expand a surveillance network
articles.summary: Kroger’s proposed acquisition of Giant Eagle could help expand its data on customers that can be used for surveillance pricing or retail advertising, says a new advocacy group report.
articles.body: Kroger’s $1.65 billion proposed acquisition of Giant Eagle might not only consolidate the grocery market, but also a vast surveillance network that includes Flock cameras, a new report warns. Beyond standard concerns that a merger could decrease competition and increase prices, the American Economic Liberties Project (AELP), which advocates for competition policy reforms, says that the consolidation could also expand customer surveillance by a single company. It comes at a time where Americans are particularly on-edge about surveillance technologies like Flock cameras and surveillance pricing, heading into a midterm election largely defined by affordability issues. A combined Kroger-Giant Eagle — which would add Giant Eagle’s 200-plus stores to Kroger’s 2,700 — could pose risks in two ways, according to AELP. The first is by enabling Kroger to acquire data on customers across a broader geographic area, which it can use to serve customers personalized pricing based on inferences about their backgrounds and shopping behaviors. It could also use that data to fuel its retail media arm, which repackages consumer insights for other brands. The second is by expanding or combining an existing physical surveillance network consisting of technologies like Flock cameras and Cooler Screens, a company that previously touted its ability to scan shoppers’ faces but backed off that messaging after public backlash. Kroger has shared data from its Flock cameras with police in Columbus, Ohio, The Columbus Dispatch reported in August. Kroger has denied using in-store facial recognition to serve customers’ prices, but has acknowledged in its privacy policy that it uses facial recognition at some stores for security purposes. Kroger and Giant Eagle did not immediately respond to The Verge’s requests for comment. Similar privacy concerns were raised during Kroger’s earlier attempted merger with Albertsons, a much larger deal that courts blocked in late 2024 after the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general challenged it. AELP argues that the proposed merger with Giant Eagle is also deserving of scrutiny, because of the way it could significantly reduce options in places like Columbus, Ohio, and also because of Kroger’s buying patterns and incentives. They urge the FTC and Ohio attorney general to seek to block the merger, though experts have predicted they might not, both because of the relatively small size of the deal compared to Albertsons, and the Trump administration’s more open approach to settlement deals than the prior administration.“Buying bleach or yogurt now comes with the prospect of being scanned, tracked, and profiled,” the report says. “With every store Kroger buys, the data and surveillance apparatus grows.”

articles.title: The Fed is expected to hold rates steady. How will Warsh justify that in the face of higher inflation?
articles.summary: Prices heated back up in September, complicating the Fed's task.
articles.body:
The Federal Reserve is widely anticipated to hold interest rates steady Wednesday afternoon, less than a week before the midterm elections . A key question: How will Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh rationalize holding rates steady after the latest inflation reports have shown prices heating back up?

Deutsche Bank chief US economist Matt Luzzetti expects Warsh will signal that recent inflation data reinforces the need for further rate hikes over time , but that skipping October allows officials more time to assess trends. However, he noted that Warsh will need to avoid making the mistake he made at his July press conference, when he created confusion about whether the Fed was committed to a credible strategy to bring down inflation.

"Warsh will want to avoid any indications that the Fed is unwilling to take appropriate action against sticky inflation," Luzzetti said.

The latest inflation reports showed prices heated back up in September, as the Consumer Price Index accelerated to 3.7% from a year earlier. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, ticked up to 2.6%, while wholesale prices jumped more than 6% and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the core Personal Consumption Expenditures Price index — is projected to top 3%.

Evercore ISI's Krishna Guha expects Warsh will explain a rate hold by saying the central bank is focused on trends, not individual data points, and that there's a lag from when rates go into place and when their impact is fully felt.

While many Fed officials have signaled they favor raising rates further to rein in inflation, others, including Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams, have indicated that there's no urgency , even if more hikes are likely, and that hikes don't need to come at consecutive meetings.

"Ideally, [Warsh] will reiterate the message from his deputies that the committee is biased to hike but wants to take a little more time to observe the impact of the last hike on the economy," JPMorgan chief economist Michael Feroli said.

Feroli thinks the center of the Fed's rate-setting committee does not think that the Fed needs to pursue a vigorous tightening cycle. Though he noted that Warsh will have to explain why the Fed hiked in September after core PCE rose 0.2% in August but is expected to rise further in September by 0.3%.

"A decision to leave rates unchanged less than a week before the midterm elections that goes unexplained would only encourage thoughts that policy is being driven by considerations other than employment and inflation," Feroli said.

articles.title: TSA finds sharp object straight out of horror movie at airport security checkpoint
articles.summary: TSA officers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport spotted Wolverine-style claws on an X-ray, calling it the most unusual find they've made in two years.
articles.body: Officers conducting a routine security screening at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) uncovered a chilling object that seemed straight out of a horror movie. While reviewing X-ray images, Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officers spotted a suspicious object that looked like a cross between Wolverine-style claws and Freddy Krueger blades, officials said. "I saw three blades and distinct claw-like features," Officer Douglas Linn said in a report on the agency's website published on Oct. 27. "I was amazed, and even more so when it came out of the bag. I have never seen anything like this during my two years at TSA." SHARP WEAPON DISCOVERED BY TSA TUCKED INSIDE UNUSUAL ITEM IN PASSENGER'S CARRY-ON BAG Officer Dennis Oishi, who was the property search officer, conducted a bag search and quickly confirmed there was a dangerous object inside. The TSA shared an Instagram post about the object. Fox News Digital reached out to TSA for additional information. What looked like a replica weapon from a movie set was quickly discovered. "In my seven years with TSA, this is one of the most unusual items I have encountered. My first thought was, ‘Oh my gosh,’ and my second thought was, ‘Is this what I think it is?’" Responding Supervisory TSA Officer Ann Rhoades said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "When Dennis asked the passenger if there was anything sharp in the bag, he said he wasn’t sure. Obviously, there was," Rhoades added. The passenger voluntarily removed the object from the bag. "Officers Linn and Oishi demonstrated the vigilance, teamwork and professionalism that define TSA’s mission every day," said Robert Spinden, Seattle TSA's federal security director. "Their actions prevented a prohibited item from moving beyond the checkpoint and reinforced the importance of careful screening, clear coordination and calm execution," Spinden continued. "I’m proud of their attention to detail and their commitment to keeping the traveling public safe." A routine security screening at upstate New York's Watertown International Airport (ART) took a startling turn when TSA officers discovered a spent smoke grenade hidden inside an aerosol container in a passenger's carry-on bag. The discovery was made by TSA officers recently, according to a Sept. 24 release from the agency. At Tampa International Airport, TSA officers discovered a 4-inch, double-edged knife concealed inside a baseball bat-shaped flashlight, the agency's website reported. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ TSA Officer Andrew Carter was screening the passenger's carry-on bag with an X-ray machine when he noticed something unusual about the flashlight and flagged the bag for a closer look. "The makeup and composition of the flashlight appeared unusual and outside what I typically expect, so I determined it required further examination," Carter said in the published note. Supervisory TSA Officer Michael Slaughter then searched the bag and felt a mass beneath its lining. After opening the lining, he found the baseball bat-shaped flashlight and noticed a line along its shaft. articles.title: Meta says it’ll probably delay its controversial new business terms again
articles.summary: Meta says it could delay the implementation of its new business terms beyond November 20th as it addresses concerns from publishers.
articles.body: Meta says it may push the implementation of its new business terms past November 20th as it faces backlash from publishers over concerns about AI training. In a post on X, Meta communications head Andy Stone said the company does “not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders.” The new business terms, which were supposed to take effect on October 30th, initially appeared to give Meta permission to train its AI models on the news sites that use Facebook and Instagram. Meta later changed its policies to remove language indicating that it could “train” its products on content scraped from these sites, but legal experts told Nieman Lab that the update still isn’t enough to rule out that possibility. Meta responded to these concerns by delaying the implementation of its terms until November 20th. Now, enforcement may be delayed indefinitely. “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update,” Stone said. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.” Along with pushback from the News/Media Alliance, lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have spoken out about the new terms. Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) said the updated terms indicate Meta is “attempting to exploit American creators and businesses,” while Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) urged Meta to reverse the change.

articles.title: ‘Was literally shaking’: Woman catches man recording her inside Metro in Bengaluru
articles.summary: Bengaluru police hunt software engineer accused of recording a 31-year-old woman on Metro near Whitefield; FIR filed for stalking under Section 78.
articles.body: Bengaluru: City police have launched a manhunt for a man who allegedly recorded a video of a 31-year-old woman commuter inside a moving Metro train in Whitefield Tuesday evening.Kadugodi police identified the suspect as Santosh T, a senior software engineer at a private tech firm in Mahadevapura and a resident of Nagarabavi. According to police, Santosh has switched off his mobile and is unresponsive. “Different police teams visited his office as well as house, but he was not available. We think his advocates will approach us soon,” a senior police officer said.Complainant R Sowpika, a private company employee from Kadugodi, said she noticed the stranger recording her video on his mobile while commuting between Kundalahalli and Hopefarm Metro stations. “The incident took place around 4.15pm. He was around 5.5 feet in height, wore blue jeans, brown t-shirt and sported a white cap. Through his illegal act, the man has violated my privacy and caused mental trauma,” Sowpika stated in her complaint.Prior to the complaint, Sowpika recorded the video while confronting the man. The video, which went viral on social media, shows Sowpika asking the man to show his mobile as she was sure of recording. In reply, the man denies it.Sowpika then sought the help of a woman security personnel in getting the man’s mobile. As the talks were on, Sowpika succeeds in grabbing the man’s phone and hands it over to the security guard.Sowpika gives him the phone, asking him to unlock it. But the man refuses and quickly drops the phone into his pocket and flees. Accompanied by Metro staff, the woman visited the jurisdictional Kadugodi police station where she registered an FIR Tuesday night.“We have booked the suspect under section 78 (Stalking). The punishment under this section is imprisonment up to three years and fine,” a police officer said.Later, Sowpika posted another video, thanking Kadugodi police. “Police were very kind and helpful. articles.title: House Democrat warns about Musk, other ‘weird trillionaires’ controlling AI
articles.summary: Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.) on Wednesday morning issued a stark warning about the influence that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other artificial intelligence technology leaders have over global affairs following a recent reported slowdown of the satellite company’s technology in Ukraine. “We’re in this world where, you know, five weird trillionaires are going to control…
articles.body:
Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.) on Wednesday morning issued a stark warning about the influence that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other artificial intelligence technology leaders have over global affairs following a recent reported slowdown of the satellite company’s technology in Ukraine.

“We’re in this world where, you know, five weird trillionaires are going to control the technology that guides and challenges our lives and livelihoods,” Himes said on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.”

The Connecticut lawmaker, who serves as the top Democrat on the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, referenced Musk’s reported decision to slow down Ukraine’s access to his company’s Starlink satellite technology. The country’s leader, Volodymyr Zelensky, said the action impaired Ukraine’s defense capabilities against Russia.

“We’re going to get to the bottom of what exactly happened that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of Ukrainians,” Himes said. “I don’t know if it was Elon. Every government entity I talk to says, ‘We didn’t dial it back.’ We’ll get to the bottom of that.”

Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials announced Saturday that the country’s Starlink defense mechanisms had been restored to normal operating speeds.

However, the incident raised questions about the power that private business leaders, like Musk, have over defense technology. Democratic lawmakers are now calling for an investigation into the SpaceX CEO.

“Elon Musk should be compelled to testify before Congress and under oath,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) wrote on social media last week in response to a Wall Street Journal report that Musk ordered the slowdown.

“National security decisions should be made in our national security interests, and not based on the personal whim of an unstable executive,” the California Democrat added.

Musk appeared to admit responsibility for authorizing the slowdown in a social media post Saturday, alleging that the Ukrainian military “violated Starlink terms of service” after it used the technology “for offensive drone strikes to kill people.”

The tech CEO specified that the U.S. government and President Trump have ultimate authority over the company’s military Starshield service, but not Starlink, the civilian version.

“SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR,” Musk wrote in the post. “That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell.”

articles.title: Ex-Google CEO: China is 6 months behind US on AI and has ‘infinite energy’
articles.summary: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said China is now just six months behind the U.S. in the global race to develop AI, warning that China has a major advantage when it comes to energy. In an interview with Fast Company released Wednesday, Schmidt said the gap between the two countries has narrowed dramatically over the…
articles.body:
Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said China is now just six months behind the U.S. in the global race to develop AI , warning that China has a major advantage when it comes to energy.

In an interview with Fast Company released Wednesday, Schmidt said the gap between the two countries has narrowed dramatically over the past two years, despite U.S. restrictions on China’s access to advanced computer chips.

“A year or two ago, it looked like China was a year or two behind. Now it looks like they’re six months behind, and there are many studies that show this,” Schmidt said.

The ex-Google chief, who helped advocate for the chip restrictions, said he initially believed they would slow China’s progress for about a decade. Instead, Chinese developers have found ways to build competitive AI systems using substantially less energy and computing power.

“I assumed they would work for about 10 years,” he said.

Schmidt said the U.S. still has the upper hand in advanced chips, talent and access to capital, but he argued that China has a significant advantage in building the infrastructure needed to support AI development.

“China has infinite energy, most of it renewable, something we said we were going to do in our country 10 years ago and failed to do,” he said.

He pointed to China’s rapid construction of data centers and power infrastructure, while American developers face lengthy delays connecting new facilities to the electrical grid.

“They don’t have interconnection queue waits that go on seven years. They don’t have the same kind of debates. They’re building the data centers, and they’re building them massively,” Schmidt said.

He estimated the U.S. will need between 60 gigawatts and 80 gigawatts of power by 2030 or 2031 to keep pace with AI demand, with each gigawatt costing roughly $50 billion.

“What we don’t have is the energy, and we don’t have the data centers,” he said.

His remarks come as the rapid expansion of AI data centers faces growing scrutiny over concerns about rising electricity costs and pressure on local water supplies.

Democratic lawmakers have already begun investigating the industry’s energy demands. Earlier this month, Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) released a report examining how data centers could drive up costs.

The scrutiny could intensify if Democrats regain control of Congress in November, with lawmakers signaling plans to pursue tougher AI safety regulations and investigations into major technology companies.

articles.title: Meta, Snap head back to LA court for social media addiction trial: What to know
articles.summary: The social media giants Meta and Snap are heading back to court this week for the latest trial in a lawsuit that alleges their platforms were intentionally designed to be addictive for young users. Jury selection begins in Los Angeles Superior Court on Wednesday for a case brought by two teenage plaintiffs referred to as…
articles.body:
The social media giants Meta and Snap are heading back to court this week for the latest trial in a lawsuit that alleges their platforms were intentionally designed to be addictive for young users.

Jury selection begins in Los Angeles Superior Court on Wednesday for a case brought by two teenage plaintiffs referred to as S.J. and K.D.B. The plaintiffs argue the design of the companies’ social media platforms caused or contributed to “serious mental health injuries they suffered as adolescents.”

The bellwether case is among the thousands of claims brought against social media companies over the design of their platforms in recent years. The slated trial will mark the third of its kind this year.

Trial consolidates claims from two plaintiffs

According to attorneys for S.J., the teenager from Illinois started using Snapchat at a young age, accessing app features like “Snapstreaks” and “Snapscore,” along with filters and push notifications. These features, attorneys allege, played a role in her compulsive use of Snapchat and played a role in S.J.’s depression, eating disorder, anxiety and self-harm.

Like S.J., K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, said she started using Instagram and Snapchat as a child. Citing features like streaks, endless scrolling, view counts and likes, K.D.B. alleges the products worsened her mental health, playing a role in her eating disorder, suicidal thoughts, depression and self-harm.

Both plaintiffs also sued TikTok and YouTube but reached settlements with the platforms in the weeks ahead of the trial. Meta and S.J. also reached a settlement last week, her attorneys said.

The platforms “intentionally designed their products to maximize users’ screen time, using complex algorithms designed to exploit human psychology and driven by advanced computer algorithms and artificial intelligence available to two of the largest technology companies in the world,” attorneys wrote in the complaint shared with The Hill.

“Defendants have progressively modified their products to promote problematic and excessive use that they know threatens the actuation of addictive and self-destructive behavioral patterns” they added.

Opening statements are expected to begin on Nov. 4, and the trial is expected to last through mid-December, according to attorneys. The case will be tried before Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn Kuhl.

Meta and Snap asked Kuhl to split the lawsuits into two separate trials, but no ruling was released ahead of Wednesday.

As seen in other online kids safety trials this year, the Los Angeles jury will hear testimony from multiple tech executives, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel and Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, next month.

This will mark Zuckerberg’s second appearance in Los Angeles just 10 months after he testified in the first bellwether case that Meta eventually lost. While on the stand last February, the CEO was grilled on young people’s use of Instagram and whether he believes Meta’s platforms deliberately addict and harm children.

Just a day before Meta reached a landmark settlement with nearly every attorney general in the country in August, Mosseri took the stand, telling the court Meta introduced a “Take A Break” pop-up feature on Instagram in 2021 to help teens control their time spent on the app, but it had lower uptake than the executive hoped.

Zuckerberg was supposed to testify in this trial, but the settlement was reached ahead of his appearance.

While Spiegel has testified in high-profile congressional hearings, his expected appearance will mark his first trial testimony.

Ahead of the trial’s start Wednesday, a Snapchat spokesperson stated Snapchat was “built differently” from traditional social media platforms, arguing the claims “fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences” on the platform.

Snapchat “opens to a camera, not a feed, not a ranking of what other people post or other social comparison metrics,” the spokesperson said. “We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources, and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first.”

Snap said its argument is backed up by independent research, citing a study from the University of Amsterdam that found Snapchat was the only major social media platform to have a positive impact on adolescent well-being and friendship closeness.

A spokesperson for Meta said the firm disagrees with the allegations, writing in a statement to The Hill, “A young person’s mental health is shaped by many factors, as the evidence in this trial will show. The plaintiff used TikTok far more than Instagram or Facebook, and her personal circumstances were a substantial factor in her struggles.”

The latest trial is following a similar playbook used earlier this year by winning plaintiffs, who targeted the social media companies over the design of the platforms, rather than the content posted by users.

Tech firms have typically avoided liability thanks to Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which largely protects them from being held legally responsible for third-party or user content. This 1996 provision was written ahead of the creation of most social media.

Meta lost two back-to-back kids online safety trials last March, including in New Mexico, where the company was ordered to pay the state $567 million. A day after this decision, a California jury determined in a separate case that Meta and YouTube were negligent in their design or operation of the platforms and ordered the companies to pay a combined $6 million.

The verdicts sent a warning shot to Big Tech , as they marked the first time juries found the social media platforms liable for their impact on kids and teens. Legal experts told The Hill the successful verdicts could pave the way for trials to get past the Section 230 shield.

Since then, several social media firms have settled similar cases before they could reach the court. Weeks before a trial slated for June, Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat settled a suit alleging the firms intentionally designed platforms to keep kids engaged, prompting mental health issues.

And in August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement for similar claims, ending a high-profile trial that was already underway in California. The settlement involved 47 U.S. states, three territories and the District of Columbia after Meta said it approached “nearly every state” to collaborate on a safety framework.

The settlement includes a monetary payment of up to $17 billion dispersed to the states over the next decade. The money goes to state efforts to prevent or reduce mental health or other harms associated with social media use. Meta also agreed to pay Texas more than $1 billion over similar allegations .

The company also agreed to set default daily time limits of two hours for users younger than 18 that can only be lifted by a parent, and it introduced blocks during the nighttime and blocked notifications during school hours.

Meta’s spokesperson touted these changes, stating the company “hopes the rest of our industry joins us in setting this new standard.”

articles.title: Right-wing activist James O’Keefe charged with unlawful voting, identity theft
articles.summary: Conservative influencer James O’Keefe was charged Wednesday in Minnesota after he and fellow right-leaning commentator Cam Higby misrepresented themselves using registered voters’ names at polling places during the state’s primary election in August. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced during a press conference the two men are facing felony unlawful voting and identity fraud charges.…
articles.body:
Conservative influencer James O’Keefe was charged Wednesday in Minnesota after he and fellow right-leaning commentator Cam Higby misrepresented themselves using registered voters’ names at polling places during the state’s primary election in August.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced during a press conference the two men are facing felony unlawful voting and identity fraud charges.

“Elections are the bedrock of democracy and their protection is one of our highest priorities,” Moriarty said in a statement . “Individuals engaging in unlawful conduct related to our elections will be held accountable.”

On the state’s Aug. 11 primary election day, O’Keefe and Higby donned mock “ Muslim attire ” and spoke in fake accents at Minnesota polling places. The two men filmed their interactions and were attempting to showcase alleged weaknesses associated with a state law that permits Minnesota voters to vouch for people who have recently moved to an area and allow them to cast ballots if they are not yet registered to vote.

The state’s vouching process requires that registered voters sign an oath confirming the address of the prospective voter. O’Keefe and Higby began the process of vouching under fake names but did not ultimately sign this oath or cast a vote, according to the county attorney.

Moriarty noted during the Wednesday press conference the vouching process is used in rare instances, accounting for 0.6 percent of votes cast in the state in the 2024 election.

“It is primarily used — and this is understandable, obviously — by senior citizens who are living in a place they just haven’t updated their license, because maybe they don’t drive anymore, so it’s not used … that much,” she said.

Moriarty pointed to felony penalties associated with improperly signing this oath as a “strong deterrent for people not to misuse the vouching process.”

“There are safeguards here,” she said. “If you sign that oath and you are lying about it or misrepresenting it, it is a felony.”

The county attorney noted the charges were not related to the men’s costumes or the political motivations behind their attempt.

“None of that played a role,” she told reporters. “The fundamental issue here is you cannot go into a polling place and misidentify yourself and use other people’s identity and say that to our election judges as you apply for a ballot, whether or not you intend to vote.”

The charges come less than a week before midterm Election Day — timing Moriarty said was coincidental. The men will be issued a summons to appear in Minnesota court.

The county attorney urged voters to consult the Minnesota secretary of State’s website for guidelines on what actions are permitted in polling places and emphasized her office’s commitment to identifying unlawful conduct in voting.

“To the citizens of Hennepin County, I encourage you to use your voice, make a plan and vote,” she said. “Take part in this election and know that we are prepared to hold anyone accountable who engages in unlawful activity related to our elections.”

The Hill has reached out to O’Keefe and Higby for comment.

articles.title: HHS to allow sale of unapproved peptides under review
articles.summary: The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture and sell peptides that have not yet been added to the list of approved substances, advancing access to those championed by the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda. The HHS stated in a notice that it would be practicing enforcement discretion…
articles.body:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture and sell peptides that have not yet been added to the list of approved substances, advancing access to those championed by the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda.

The HHS stated in a notice that it would be practicing enforcement discretion — upholding only certain regulations or disciplinary actions — when it comes to manufacturing and selling of the peptides BPC-157, TB-500, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c and Semax.

This decision essentially gives compounding pharmacies the go-ahead to sell those six peptides without having to worry about regulatory pushback from federal agencies. State-level rules on what and how much compounding pharmacies can make differ and potentially clash with federal rules.

These are the same peptides that the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted in favor of allowing the pharmacies to make and sell, despite evaluations by FDA scientists finding that there was not enough evidence to support claims that these substances helped with certain conditions.

The Trump administration said the move would “expand and improve patient access while FDA reviews these substances, in the circumstances below, HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using” one of the peptides it cited on Tuesday.

Earlier this month, the FDA submitted an “interim access policy” to the White House for review, though details of the policy were not made available at the time.

In its notice, the HHS acknowledged these peptides are not FDA-approved, evaluated for safety and may even “pose risks to patients,” but it stated the decision by the PCAC indicated “significant interest” in peptide use.

Last year, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. added numerous new members to the committee, several of whom own wellness clinics or pharmacies and are ideologically aligned with Kennedy’s favorable views on peptides.

articles.title: 50,000 airline miles stolen from a travel expert
articles.summary: Travel expert Katy Nastro says 50,000 American Airlines AAdvantage miles vanished from her account after someone redeemed them without permission.
articles.body: If you're anything like me, you've probably spent years collecting airline miles, dreaming about the trip you'll eventually take. Maybe it's a business class seat to Europe or that vacation you've been putting off. You keep earning points and watching the balance grow. But what happens when you finally check your account and discover someone else has already spent them? That's exactly what happened to Katy Nastro, a travel expert with Flighty, a flight-tracking app that provides real-time updates on delays, cancellations and gate changes. During our conversation on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast, Katy shared how more than 50,000 American Airlines miles vanished from her account. Someone had redeemed them for a flight without her permission. What surprised me was that Katy knows the travel industry inside and out. Yet she still found herself dealing with a problem that could happen to anyone with a frequent flyer account. Her experience offers a warning, especially as holiday travel approaches. 9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET/8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. How a travel expert discovered 50,000 stolen airline miles Katy had just landed in New York and was riding home in an Uber. Like many frequent travelers, she opened her American Airlines app to check how many miles she'd earned from her latest trip. Instead, she noticed a substantial drop in her balance. At first, she figured the app had made a mistake. She remembered redeeming about 10,000 miles recently, but the balance was off by roughly 50,000. So she refreshed the app. The missing miles were still missing. That's when she called American Airlines. The airline told her that someone had redeemed the miles for a ticket in another person's name. Katy had been saving for a trip to Asia. Unfortunately, those miles were now associated with a flight she knew nothing about. "I really had this just stomach drop moment," Katy told me. She had spent years earning those rewards, including through long flights to Australia. Suddenly, someone else had benefited from all that travel. "I naively never thought this could happen to me because I work in the industry," she admitted. I found that particularly revealing. Katy had previously warned people about loyalty account theft. Even with that experience, she never expected to become a victim herself. Getting stolen airline miles back was surprisingly complicated You might assume the airline could simply reverse an unauthorized redemption. After all, the ticket was booked in someone else's name. Unfortunately, Katy discovered that getting her miles back required additional work. American Airlines instructed her to submit a formal fraud complaint by email. She also had to file a police report and provide documentation before the airline would restore her miles. "I had to have the police report filed with them before anything was credited," Katy explained. She eventually recovered her miles, but the process didn't end there. Katy also had to create a new email address and establish a replacement American Airlines AAdvantage account. Thankfully, the airline transferred her existing status along with her restored rewards. What caught my attention was the police report requirement. Katy had to involve local law enforcement even though the theft happened entirely online. She understood why the airline might want official documentation, but she questioned whether the process needed to be so cumbersome. There's another concern for travelers. Airline loyalty points generally don't carry the same protections as money stolen through an unauthorized credit card purchase. In fact, American Airlines' current AAdvantage terms say the airline has no general obligation to restore miles withdrawn without authorization. The company may review requests submitted within three months of the unauthorized withdrawal, but reimbursement remains discretionary. That makes discovering suspicious activity quickly especially important. Also, keep in mind that each loyalty program has its own fraud procedures. A police report may be requested, but the requirement isn't universal. How thieves turn stolen airline miles into real trips I asked Katy something that had been bothering me. Who was actually flying around using her miles? She had no idea. The airline identified a redemption involving someone else's name, but Katy didn't know who was behind it or where the traveler was headed. Loyalty programs often allow members to book tickets for other people. Some also permit mileage transfers or gifts. Those legitimate features can create opportunities for criminals who gain unauthorized access to an account. For example, someone who controls your account could redeem miles for a ticket under another person's name. Depending on the program, the points might also be transferred or exchanged for other rewards. However, Katy never learned exactly how someone accessed her account. During our conversation, she acknowledged that password reuse may have played a role. "I think I fell into the trap of using the same password for everything," she said. That's an easy habit to fall into. If criminals obtain a password from one compromised service, they may try using it to access other accounts. And here's something worth remembering. A loyalty balance may look like a collection of numbers on your screen, but those numbers can pay for expensive flights. Why saving airline miles forever could cost you Katy shared another piece of advice that might surprise anyone who's been patiently saving miles for years. She believes travelers should think twice about holding on to their rewards indefinitely. "I would highly suggest that you should not be waiting on those miles," she told me. Her concern comes down to depreciation. Airlines can change their award pricing, which means a flight that once required 50,000 miles might eventually require considerably more. I compared holding on to miles to buying a new car and watching its value drop after driving off the lot. Katy agreed. In her view, people often wait too long for that perfect first-class redemption. She recommends considering redemptions within a year instead of endlessly saving for a future trip. Of course, you still want to check whether an award flight offers reasonable value. Spending 80,000 miles on an inexpensive economy ticket could be a poor deal. However, if you need to travel during a busy holiday period, using miles for an economy seat may make sense. Award tickets can also offer more flexibility than certain restrictive cash fares. Just check the airline's cancellation and redeposit rules before booking. We've shared more strategies in our article, Are airline miles still worth it? And if you're looking to earn more rewards for your next trip, check out my picks for the best airline credit cards of 2026 at CyberGuy.com to see which programs might work best for you. YOUR CREDIT CAN LOOK NORMAL WHILE SOMEONE STEALS YOUR IDENTITY Watch out for fake airline alerts and customer service scams During our conversation, I told Katy about something I've been seeing more frequently. I receive emails that look like legitimate airline notifications, claiming miles were redeemed from my account. Some are convincing enough that I've nearly clicked them myself. That's a particularly sneaky approach because many airlines send real notifications when members redeem rewards. Criminals can imitate those messages to create panic and lure people toward fake login pages. Katy warned that scammers also create fake airline support accounts on social media. Someone looking for help with a delayed flight or missing miles might contact what appears to be an official account. The conversation can then move to a private message or even WhatsApp, where the criminal asks for personal information. Katy's warning was clear. Avoid sharing sensitive account information through social media conversations. If you receive a suspicious redemption notice, open the airline's official app yourself. Check your account activity directly rather than following links in the message. How to protect your airline miles and hotel points Before your next trip, take a few minutes to secure the loyalty accounts you've spent years building. These steps can help you spot unauthorized activity sooner and make your accounts harder to compromise. 1) Check your rewards balances regularly Open your airline and hotel loyalty apps at least once a month. Review recent redemptions and compare your current balance with what you expected. Katy said she sometimes went several months without checking her account. That made it harder to know when the unauthorized redemption occurred. Setting a recurring calendar reminder can help you catch unusual activity sooner. Also, enable account activity and redemption alerts if your loyalty program offers them. That way, you may find out about suspicious transactions before you notice missing miles. 2) Give every loyalty account a unique password Never reuse your airline password on another website. A password manager can generate strong, unique passwords and store them securely. Also, protect the email account connected to your loyalty program. Someone who gains access to that inbox may be able to reset your rewards password. 3) Enable extra account security when available Look for two-factor authentication (2FA), passkeys or other login verification options offered by your airline or hotel program. These protections vary by provider, so check your account's security settings. Also, review any unfamiliar changes to your contact information and remove devices or sessions you no longer recognize when the service allows it. 4) Be cautious with unexpected redemption alerts If an email or text claims someone used your points, resist clicking its links. Instead, open the official airline app or type the website address into your browser. Legitimate-looking logos and familiar formatting offer no guarantee that a message is genuine. Also, be skeptical of anyone claiming to represent airline support through an unsolicited social media message. Use strong antivirus software to help detect malicious links, block dangerous websites and protect against malware designed to steal your passwords. While antivirus software can't stop every phishing scam, it provides an additional layer of protection if you accidentally click something suspicious. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS 5) Report missing miles immediately Contact your loyalty program through its verified customer service channels as soon as you notice an unauthorized redemption. Ask the airline to secure your account and investigate the transaction. Save your account statements and any correspondence. If the airline requests a police report, follow its instructions and keep a copy. Don't delay because some programs impose deadlines on fraud claims. 6) Consider a separate email for travel accounts Katy suggested using a dedicated email address for loyalty programs. That can make account notifications easier to track and reduce exposure if an unrelated service suffers a breach. Another option is to use an email alias, which helps keep your primary address private. It lets you create unlimited email aliases, helping you organize travel accounts while reducing spam and unwanted exposure. You can also follow my guide on how to create and use email aliases. For recommendations on private and secure email providers that offer alias addresses, visit CyberGuy.com. 7) Use a personal data removal service Your personal information may already be circulating on data broker websites, making it easier for scammers to target you with convincing airline phishing emails or impersonation attempts. Consider using a personal data removal service. It helps remove your personal information from hundreds of data broker and people search sites and continues submitting removal requests when your details reappear. While no service can erase everything or directly prevent someone from stealing your airline miles, reducing your online exposure can make it harder for scammers to gather personal details and tailor their attacks. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 8) Keep your boarding passes and loyalty numbers private Be careful about sharing photos of boarding passes, luggage tags or travel confirmations online. These documents can contain booking reference numbers, frequent flyer details or barcodes that expose information about your trip. Criminals may use those details to access reservations or impersonate travelers. Avoid posting travel documents on social media, and securely dispose of printed boarding passes after your trip. 9) Set up an AI alert for changes to your airline miles You can use an AI assistant like ChatGPT with scheduled tasks to monitor airline loyalty programs for changes that could reduce the value of your miles. Set up a daily alert to check for announced changes to redemption rates, award pricing or loyalty program rules. You can even ask it to track news about American Airlines AAdvantage or other programs you use. That way, you may hear about upcoming changes while there's still time to redeem your miles at current rates. Keep in mind that airlines don't always announce devaluations in advance, so AI can't predict every change. Kurt's key takeaways I keep thinking about Katy sitting in the back of that Uber, casually checking her mileage balance and discovering that 50,000 hard-earned miles had disappeared. I've collected airline miles for years, and I know how much planning goes into using them. The thought of some stranger enjoying a trip on my points would make me furious. What concerns me even more is that Katy works in the travel industry and still couldn't explain exactly how someone got into her account. That tells me we should give our loyalty accounts the same attention we give our financial accounts. Check your balances, use unique passwords and pay attention to unusual activity. And while I love saving miles for a great trip, Katy makes a convincing argument for enjoying those rewards while they still offer good value. articles.title: Instagram now testing videos up to 90 minutes long in major shift
articles.summary: One major question remains: Will Instagram compensate creators for their videos the way YouTube does?
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — Instagram is moving beyond its signature short-form videos, testing a new feature that allows creators to share content lasting up to 90 minutes, including podcasts, interviews and comedy shows.

The Meta-owned platform announced Monday that it is testing a feature called “Features,” which allows select creators to upload longer, horizontal videos that viewers can watch directly within the app.

“For a long time, I have been against doing long-form video on Instagram,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri said in a video posted Monday alongside Tessa Lyons, the company’s vice president of product. “But we are actually gonna lean in for a bunch of different reasons.”

Lyons, who previously led product development for Instagram Reels, described the expansion as a new chapter for the platform.

“It feels like a full-circle moment that we’re here now talking about the beginning of our journey on long-form video,” she said.

Rather than leaving Instagram to watch a full podcast or interview elsewhere, users will be able to tap a short clip and continue watching the longer version directly within the app.

“You’re basically scrolling through. You’ll see that vertical video, and then it says, ‘Hey, do you want to tap to watch the full video?'” Nexstar’s Rich DeMuro explained Tuesday morning.

Viewers who tap the prompt are taken to the longer, horizontal version of the video.

“You can even send these videos to your TV to watch on a bigger screen,” DeMuro said.

Instagram is also developing tools to help creators connect their short-form clips with full-length videos.

In a separate interview with creators Colin Rosenblum and Samir Chaudry, Mosseri explained how podcasters currently use Instagram to promote longer content hosted elsewhere.

“You slice it up, you use platforms like Instagram as the top of funnel to raise awareness and then you kind of go to, you know, a podcast player or YouTube or wherever to watch the full-length thing,” Mosseri said.

Under the new approach, viewers will be able to watch the entire video without leaving Instagram.

Creators can link up to eight short clips to a single longer video, according to Variety , giving audiences multiple ways to discover full episodes.

The feature was previously tested in Brazil and is now expanding to select creators in the United States, according to The Hollywood Reporter .

The company is also expanding Instagram for TV, allowing users to watch videos on larger screens through Apple TV, Samsung, Amazon Fire TV and Google TV.

The expansion comes as YouTube has become a major destination for video podcasts and other long-form entertainment.

Instagram is also testing “Series,” a feature designed to organize episodes of recurring shows, and expanding the ways users can discover livestreams.

“Our goal is really to be the best place for social entertainment,” Lyons told Bloomberg in an interview published by the Los Angeles Times .

“To do that well, we need to broaden the way that we enable people to tell stories through video and enable audiences to discover them,” she added.

Will Instagram pay creators like YouTube?

One major question remains: Will Instagram compensate creators for their videos the way YouTube does?

YouTube, which is owned by Google, offers eligible creators a share of advertising revenue, but Instagram has not announced a comparable program for its new long-form videos.

An Instagram spokesperson told Variety that the company is providing funding directly to some creators but has not finalized a long-term payment model.

Mosseri has also acknowledged that previous attempts to introduce broader creator payments were costly and did not produce the results the company had hoped for, according to Business Insider .

For now, Features remains in testing, and Instagram has not announced when the 90-minute video option will become available to all creators.

articles.body:
Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the ranking member on the House Intelligence Committee, said Wednesday that the use of paper ballots prevents hacking from tech mogul Elon Musk, who is supporting Republicans this election cycle.

“Forty-nine of the 50 states have paper records of the ballots, right?” Himes said on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.”

“Except for Louisiana, every other state in the union has a paper backup,” he added. “So, let’s just imagine that Elon Musk or whoever can pull off something they’ve never pulled off before and get in and change the vote totals, it would be relatively easy to go back and check that against the actual paper ballot.”

Musk, an ally of President Trump, has spent more than $442 million in the midterm elections, after putting an additional $76.8 million into his super PAC in the past month. Between July and September, the tech mogul gave a combined $276 million to his super PAC and various Republican groups.

Musk also spent a significant amount backing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in his Senate race against Democrat James Talarico.

Officials in states around the country have recently played defense against election fraud claims from Trump, with the president doubling down ahead of this year’s midterms.

In remarks to the country in July, the president claimed to see “shocking vulnerabilities in our election infrastructure.” Trump pointed to a voter registration case in Michigan from 2020, also taking aim at California, suggesting the Golden State’s mail-in ballots were “floating aimlessly.”

Trump has a history of election denial , repeatedly claiming falsely that he won the 2020 presidential election.

articles.title: Brendan Carr plans to let prisons jam cellphone signals
articles.summary: The FCC will vote on November 19th on a proposal to allow prisons to get licenses for cellphone jamming equipment that would block inmates from using phones.
articles.body: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr announced the agency will vote on November 19th on rules that would allow prisons to use signal jamming. Radiofrequency jammers are generally banned under Section 333 and the Communications Act of 1934, with few exceptions, and Carr has noted they’ve been permitted for use at some federal facilities already. Carr claims in a statement that jammers are needed because “For years, thousands upon thousands of contraband cellphones have been pouring into prisons, and some of the worst possible offenders have been using them to order hits, coordinate violent gang activity, and aid criminal enterprises.” When the FCC approved a draft proposal last year, FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez suggested beginning with a pilot program to test the implications on surrounding areas, saying, “While the problem we are trying to address is of critical importance, I worry about the potential unintended consequences of permitting jamming by non-federal actors and permitting jamming equipment to formally enter the American market.” Arkansas AG Tim Griffin, who was also present for the event where the vote was announced, and Georgia AG Chris Carr have been among law enforcement officials pushing for the change. However, anonymous incarcerated journalists argue that this push is actually a response to their use of phones to distribute “uncensored reports of civil rights violations to news media in a timely enough manner to deny the creation of cover-ups.” They specifically cited the 2024 DOJ investigation into Georgia’s prisons that found “horrific and inhumane conditions” in response to evidence initially transferred via contraband phones. The FCC’s proposal describes how prisons could get licenses to use jamming equipment: > As the Commission takes this historic step to improve public safety, eligible entities pursuing either of the two licensing paths will be subject to technical standards and testing requirements. This includes initial testing pursuant to an experimental license to prove that the jamming solution does not cause harmful interference outside of the designated geographic areas, as well as post-license grant testing at the subject correctional facility prior to beginning operations. > Jamming may occur only within a Commission-authorized “jamming containment area” where wireless device operation is prohibited, and it must not cause harmful interference outside that area. > Additionally, relevant carriers, FirstNet, public safety coordinators, and 911 authorities would receive advance notice of the on-site testing, and nearby communities would receive notice before deployment. As Carr’s announcement notes, there are also legislative attempts to allow correctional facilities to use signal jamming technology, like the Cellphone Jamming Reform Act of 2025, introduced last year by Arkansas senator Tom Cotton.

articles.title: Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech
articles.summary: The United States has blocked future foreign routers, robots, Roombas, and drones. What’s next?
articles.body: What do drones, routers, and Roombas have in common? The US government wants to keep Chinese ones from entering the country. They’re the first consumer gadgets that are facing de facto import bans because of the US government’s xenophobic stance — and they might not be the last. Originally, the US government was just worried about US networks. It’s been distrustful of Chinese telecom equipment providers Huawei and ZTE for well over a decade, eventually requiring telecom providers to “rip and replace” their gear. (Many telecoms have still failed to do so.) It established an “Entity List” for companies whose gear should be banned from import, marketing, and sale. But under the second Trump administration, that list has been weaponized against entire home consumer gadget categories too — starting in December 2025 when Trump and Brendan Carr’s FCC banned all future foreign drones unless their companies obtained a waiver. Next was a ban on all future foreign routers, all future foreign robots and power inverters, and within the robot ban, all future foreign robovacs. In each case, the government claims it’s because those gadgets fundamentally pose an unacceptable threat to US national security. But in each case, the US has provided zero public evidence of a threat, has done nothing about existing drones and routers and robots that might pose such a threat, and hasn’t given us any reason to trust that its waivers have anything to do with security. Besides, there are rarely any US companies to fill the gaps left by foreign ones. Consumer gadgets are largely made overseas, including practically all routers and practically all drones — just like how your Apple, Dell, and HP laptops are not made in the US. In this StoryStream, we’re following the latest on the foreign gadget bans.

articles.title: Fed votes in split decision to hold interest rates steady despite sticky inflation
articles.summary: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also announced a change to the meeting schedule.
articles.body:
With the midterm elections less than a week away, the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, even as the latest inflation reports show prices rising again.

The central bank voted in a split decision to hold its benchmark interest rate steady in the range of 3.75% to 4%, after raising rates last month for the first time in more than three years.

Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack and Fed governor Lisa Cook broke ranks, preferring to raise rates by a quarter percentage point. This is the second time since July Hammack has dissented in favor of raising rates and Cook's first dissent in her tenure.

Officials said they are focused on reviewing additional data to inform future rate decisions, adjusting their policy statement to say that "the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee's 2% goal."

The latest inflation reports show price growth has accelerated since September's hike.

The Consumer Price Index clocked in at 3.7% last month from 3.4% in August. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 2.6%, compared with 2.4% in August. Wholesale prices jumped more than 6% last month, and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the core Personal Consumption Expenditures Price index, due out Thursday — is projected to top 3%.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, in a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, acknowledged that the job of containing inflation is unfinished.

"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine [is] starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said. "I'm encouraged by the progress we've made in a short period of time. But if the crux of your question is 'you haven't delivered yet, you haven't achieved price stability,' you're right about that.

Warsh announced a change to the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting schedule, beginning next year. They will still meet eight times a year, but one meeting will "focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said.

In 2028, he said, two meetings will be dedicated to strategy and six to setting policy.
