articles.title: Hacker stole personnel data about thousands of Homeland Security employees, including CBP and ICE agents | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A hacker obtained personally identifiable information about more than 40,000 Homeland Security staffers, which has since been published online.
articles.body:
Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year.

The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials.

A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access.

More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry.

The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA.

Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service.

“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out.

This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors.

The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest.

TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff .

It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment about the breach.

When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said.

Thousands of ICE agents’ access linked to web surveillance tools, online therapy

While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE.

The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work.

Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software.

The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit.

A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023.

Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media.

A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment.

One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status .

The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act.

“Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People.

“Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro.

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.”

articles.title: Trump Delays Robotics, Machinery Tariffs in Favor of More Talks
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he would hold off on imposing tariffs on imports of robotics, industrial machinery and related parts and components, instead dire...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said he would hold off on imposing tariffs on imports of robotics, industrial machinery and related parts and components, instead directing officials to hold talks with trading partners on those goods.

Trump signed a proclamation Wednesday agreeing with a Commerce Department report, which determined robotics and industrial machines are being imported in quantities and in ways that threaten US national security.

He directed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to negotiate with trading partners to address those imports and to report on their progress within 180 days, leaving the door open to subsequent tariffs.

"Depending on the status or outcome of such negotiations, I may consider alternative remedies in the future," Trump said.

The Trump administration in September 2025 announced an investigation into the imports of robotics and industrial machines, under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, which authorizes the president to impose trade restrictions on national security grounds.

The probe covered robotics and programmable, computer-controlled mechanical systems, including CNC machining centers, turning and milling machines, grinding and deburring equipment and industrial stamping and pressing machines.

Also within the scope of the investigation were "automatic tool changers, jigs and fixtures, and machine tools for cutting, welding, and handling work pieces." Specialty metalworking equipment, such as autoclaves and industrial ovens, and laser and water cutting tools and machinery were also included.

Critics have warned new levies on such imports could undercut the administration's goal of boosting US manufacturing by increasing costs.

A series of trade investigations has underpinned Trump's effort to rebuild the tariff wall struck down by the US Supreme Court earlier this year, this time using powers seen to be more legally sound. The president has targeted both imports from individual countries and broad industrial sectors.

Yet the Commerce Department has similarly held off on other tariffs even after probes found that imports threatened US security. Earlier this month, Trump delayed imposing tariffs on wind turbines and their components, giving officials time to consult with trading partners.

articles.title: Readwise is taking on Kindle and Kobo for ebook supremacy
articles.summary: Taking on Kindle is hard. Beating Goodreads might be really easy.﻿
articles.body: For the last several years, Readwise has been building tools for power readers. There’s the eponymous product, Readwise, which stores and categorizes your Kindle highlights to help you remember what you’ve read. There’s Readwise Reader, an app for reading newsletters, PDFs, and web articles you’ve saved for later. And now there’s Readwise Books, a full-fledged platform for buying, reading, and talking about books. Readwise Books is currently in beta, available through invite or to existing Readwise subscribers. I’ve been testing the app for a few days, and it’s a much bigger take on reading than most. Tristan Homsi and Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s cofounders, like to call the platform “Strava for reading” because it can track how long, how much, and how fast you read, and it can show that information to friends you make in the Readwise Books app. The app’s homepage is a feed of what other people are reading, with comments and recommendations laced throughout. “Strava for reading” wasn’t the original goal of Readwise Books, which has been part of the Readwise plan since the beginning. “Literally, Dan and I talked about this when we first met,” Homsi says. “We feel like Kindle could be so much better. We really didn’t think it would take nine-plus years to be able to get to this point.” But it turns out, Doyon adds, that for all their ideas about innovation in books, “no one sits around wanting a better Kindle.” But there is one thing they do wish for: a better Goodreads. “Everybody hates Goodreads.” In a sense, then, the plan for Readwise Books is to take on Kindle by first taking on Goodreads. The Readwise Books app offers a nice way to track books you want to read, are reading, and have read; it even syncs with your Kindle account to let you track books you’ve bought from Amazon by taking pictures of your starting and ending pages. You can rate and review books and see what others have said. It’s a little Strava, a little Letterboxd, and a lot nicer to look at than Goodreads. The long-term goal, of course, is to get people to stop buying Kindle books and start buying from Readwise. Homsi and Doyon have spent the last several years working to reach deals with all five of the major US publishers in order to have a competitive library of books available. That meant endless negotiations, security reviews, DRM debates, and more — both cofounders seem exhausted just talking about the process. But eventually, by several small miracles, they got the deals done. And since those deals govern the price of books, and many things about how they’re sold and presented, they bring Readwise to a nearly even playing field almost immediately. It all took a lot longer than expected, but Doyon and Homsi think their timing might actually be pretty good. Digital book reading continues to grow, particularly among young people; a huge amount of that reading happens on phones and tablets. Meanwhile, a new crop of E Ink devices like the tiny Xteink and the Boox Palma line have expanded the universe of available hardware for a company like Readwise. [Image: Readwise breaks your reading into “sessions,” like a workout in Strava. Not long ago, Doyon says, they would have had no choice but to build an e-reader of their own. (And he says they still might.) Now, they can just make sure it runs on an E Ink-friendly flavor of Android. After a couple of days using Readwise Books, I can say confidently I already like it better than practically all of its competition. It’s a much nicer-looking app than anything you’ll get from Kindle or Kobo; it has lots of ways to customize how books look; and at least for now, I’m finding the tracking features compel me to read more instead of annoying me. (Homsi says some early versions of the gamification features were substantially more annoying.) I’ve found a few bugs, and the half-integration with Kindle is a little confusing in spots, but it’s already a really nice place to read. Of course, I, like millions of other people, already own a Kindle and lots of Kindle books. Switching ebook platforms is hard, and Doyon says he’s not counting on everyone to do it right away. He says he’s hopeful Readwise can persuade existing users to switch, in order to sync their notes and progress more seamlessly. He’s also hoping that the advent of AI, and the ways in which AI reliance may rot our brains, will get a lot of people back into the idea of reading more deeply again. And that a bunch of those people might be looking for a nicer, more social place to do so.

articles.title: 'I didn't hear an utterance about politics': Warsh bats away midterm talk following rate decision
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Wednesday sidestepped multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.
articles.body:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.

But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters.

"I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political."

When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt.

"Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."

He had another political topic to address before it was over when he was asked about a hearing planned for next week of a White House committee investigating allegations against Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook.

It's the latest twist in the White House effort to remove Cook from the central bank. Warsh was asked if he personally or the Fed as an institution would be involved in those proceedings.

Warsh even seemed wary of weighing in on President Trump's effort to rebrand artificial intelligence (AI) as super intelligence (SI), answering a question on the topic before quickly noting, "whether you pronounce it AI or SI ... is up to you."

He defended the central bank's decision to keep interest rates steady less than a week before the midterm elections and maintained that he is determined to get inflation to 2%.

But the bevy of political questions underscored the meeting's politically fraught timing , which the Fed has had to navigate before.

The central bank raised rates in 2022 ahead of midterm voting, which Democrats blasted . The Fed then cut rates in 2024, which then-candidate Donald Trump immediately called "a political move to try and keep somebody in office."

This time, the central bank held steady. Trump didn't immediately weigh in on the merits of the decision but told reporters on Wednesday afternoon he had not spoken to Warsh about this week's decision.

Last month, the president said he had spoken to Warsh before that meeting and has long been vocal about why he thinks interest rates should be lower.

articles.title: Hegseth seeks to assuage Southeast Asian partners on trip to Philippines
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth attempted to assuage Southeast Asian partners this week that the U.S. is dedicated to its allies in the Asia-Pacific region and pitched a defense framework to guide cooperation in the next few years during his trip to the Philippines. Hegseth said the Trump administration’s “strong, quiet and clear” approach to the…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth attempted to assuage Southeast Asian partners this week that the U.S. is dedicated to its allies in the Asia-Pacific region and pitched a defense framework to guide cooperation in the next few years during his trip to the Philippines.

Hegseth said the Trump administration’s “strong, quiet and clear” approach to the Indo-Pacific means Washington is willing to defend its interests and the interests of allies and partners.

“That is, by definition, peace through strength. And we’re ready and willing to work with all of you where you are based on your own circumstances and your own priorities and shared mutual interest thereafter,” Hegseth said this week to the U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) defense ministers in Cebu, Philippines.

The Pentagon chief’s appearance in the Philippines comes as Indo-Pacific allies continue to assess the U.S. commitment to the region and the broader impacts of the U.S. war against Iran , which has dragged on for more than seven months.

Hegseth said the relationship with Indo-Pacific allies will boost interoperability, strengthen maritime domain awareness and bolster the cooperation between U.S. and partner navies.

“Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict,” Hegseth said, noting the differing views in the group.

“We’re not going to agree on everything, nor do we need to,” he continued. “But an agreement on the fundamentals is enough to support practical cooperation where our shared interests are overlapping and are clear, and that’s the type of cooperation the Department of War will continue to pursue with our ASEAN partners,” he said, using the Trump administration’s preferred name for the Department of Defense.

Hegseth did not elaborate much more about the new defense framework but noted it will guide the cooperation in the next several years, adding that the U.S. is ready to work with Singapore, which will assume the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus (ADMM-Plus) chairmanship.

The administration’s assurance to the region, with Hegseth calling the U.S. a “proud Pacific nation,” is important for the host country, the Philippines, whose tensions with China have ramped up over maritime and territorial disputes in the South China Sea and Luzon Strait.

The two nations have looked to enforce their territorial claims with aircraft and vessels.

Gregory B. Poling, who oversees the Southeast Asia Program and Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said Hegseth’s comments will be “well received” and that in many ways showing up at the ADMM-Plus meeting and not “saying anything overly concerning counts for a lot at the moment.”

“I’m sure the Philippines would have liked some more clear language on the South China Sea or Mutual Defense Treaty, and perhaps that will still come,” Poling told The Hill on Wednesday.

As for the U.S.-ASEAN defense framework, Poling said it seemed like a “floating a trial balloon more than a fully fleshed-out proposal.”

“But we’ll have to wait for Singapore’s ASEAN chairmanship next year to see if we hear about it again.”

articles.title: A hacker stole more than 40,000 DHS employee records
articles.summary: A hacker stole thousands of records from the Department of Homeland Security, revealing names, job titles, phone numbers, and emails of ICE and CBP employees.
articles.body: A hacker stole a trove of personal information from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The breach exposes the names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses, and office locations of more than 41,000 employees, including those in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), according to TechCrunch and Wired. The data also linked the agencies to specific surveillance tools. As reported by TechCrunch, a hacker known as “Department of Peace” gained access to the data through Okta, an identity and access management service used by the DHS. Around 21,000 records pertain to CBP employees, and nearly 7,000 belong to staff at ICE. The data also includes records from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). The DHS has worked to conceal the identities of CBP and ICE agents, who have carried out anti-immigration raids around the US, while also tracking down online critics. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” the “Department of Peace” hacker said, according to TechCrunch. This leak comes just weeks after hackers stole data from the FBI on its employees and job applicants. The leaked DHS information was reportedly given to cybersecurity researcher maia arson crimew, who shared it with Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a nonprofit organization that’s now hosting the leaked “Icepick” dataset. The leak also reportedly includes information about DHS groups that have access to tools that can be used for surveillance, such as the facial recognition app Mobile Fortify and PenLink, which can collect and analyze data from phones and online services. The DHS didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

articles.body:
The Federal Election Commission’s (FEC) electronic filing system was restored and online Wednesday afternoon, nearly two days after the system initially went down with little explanation.

In a post on X shortly before 5 p.m. EDT Wednesday, the FEC announced the filing system was “back online and available to filers,” adding work is continuing to restore the search feature for the filing system and the agency’s notification service.

The filing system is used by political committees, candidates, political action and party committees to submit campaign finance and reports online. The filing system outage did not impact the FEC’s website search function to find campaign donation recipients and PAC information.

It is not clear what caused the outage, though Reuters , citing an email, reported the FEC website was targeted by a hacker or hackers.

The agency first reported the outage Monday night and said it was continuing to work to resolve the issue through most of Tuesday. On Tuesday evening, the agency said the issue was “identified” and a fix was being implemented.

The incident comes just under a week until voters across the country will head to the polls for the midterm elections, though the FEC has no role in the voting and election process.

Democratic FEC Commissioner Dara Lindenbaum emphasized this during the outage Tuesday, writing on X , “Louder for those in the back!@FEC ONLY handles campaign finance reports which list raising and spending.”

“We play zero role in administering the election. We don’t receive, maintain, or come close to dealing with voter files, voting machines or voting,” she continued.

articles.body:
Nonprofit leaker collective Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets) published data Wednesday for over 40,000 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, some of whom are working in the intelligence community.

DDoSecrets did not identify the source who leaked the personnel information, referring to the unnamed individual instead as the “Department of Peace.”

“This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” a hacker and activist affiliated with the group, who goes by “maia arson crimew,” said in a statement. “It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security’s organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE.”

The hacker also released a tool that listed names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from various DHS agencies — including for Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and Homeland Security Investigations personnel.

The tool incorporated job titles and email groups , which helped to show particular agents involved with undercover work, special operations and surveillance jobs.

“It is a complete game changer for anyone investigating DHS, simplifying the identification of agents and their lines of command. It provides FOIA material for years to come,” the press released continued.

Multiple hackers affiliated with the leak targeted “the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs.”

DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best wrote that , through this leak, the group was “replacing the regime’s anonymity with accountability” which “are a catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.”

In March, the “Department of Peace” leaked 6,000 DHS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) contracts with private universities and businesses — including Palantir, Microsoft, Oracle and Anduril.

At the time of that leak, the department said in a statement, “Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I’m releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they’re working on.”

The hacks follow the department scaling up immigration enforcement operations across the country. According to numbers published in the Deportation Data Project, ICE arrested 49,571 people in July 2026 — marking its highest monthly arrest total during President Trump’s second term.

DHS did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.
